title: Epistolae
author: Jerome
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0162.stoa004.perseus-lat2, as held by the Perseus Digital Library.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit the Perseus Digital Library and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: In mea enim patria rusticitatis vernacula deus venter est et de die vivitur: sanctior est ille, qui ditior est. Accessit huic patellae iuxta tritum populi proverbium dignum operculum, Lupicinus sacerdos—secundum illud quoque, de quo semel in vita Crassum ait risisse Lucilius: Similem habent labra lactucam asino cardus comedente—videlicet ut perforatam navem debilis gubernator regat et caecus caecos ducat in foveam talisque sit rector, quales illi qui reguntur.
passages.english: For in my homeland, with its native boorishness, the belly is god and people live from day to day: the holier man is the one who is richer. To this dish, as the well-worn popular proverb has it, a fitting lid has been added: Lupicinus the priest. This also accords with that saying at which, Lucilius says, Crassus laughed once in his life: "The lips have a lettuce to match, when a donkey eats thistles." That is, a feeble helmsman steers a holed ship, the blind leads the blind into the pit, and the ruler is such as those who are ruled.
passages.notes: "Sacerdos" here may mean bishop, as often in Jerome. The Lucilius line is a proverb, "like lips, like lettuce": the donkey's lips are as rough as the thistles it eats.

passages.original: At, si tibi placet scire, quot molestiis virgo libera, quot uxor adstricta sit, lege Tertulliani ad amicum philosophum et de virginitate alios libellos et beati Cypriani volumen egregium et papae Damasi super hac re versu prosaque conposita et Ambrosii nostri quae nuper ad sororem scripsit opuscula. In quibus tanto se fudit eloquio, ut, quidquid ad laudem virginum pertinet, exquisierit, ordinant, expresserit.
passages.english: But if you would like to know how many troubles a virgin is free from and how many a wife is bound by, read Tertullian's [book] To a Philosopher Friend and his other little books on virginity, and the excellent volume of the blessed Cyprian, and what Pope Damasus composed on this subject in verse and prose, and the short works which our Ambrose recently wrote to his sister. In these he has poured himself out with such eloquence that he has sought out, set in order and expressed whatever pertains to the praise of virgins.
passages.notes: 'ordinant' is evidently a scanning error for 'ordinarit' (= ordinaverit), 'set in order'; translated so.

passages.original: AMBROSIUS, quo chartas, sumptus, notarios ministrante tam innumerabiles libros vere Adamantius et noster Χαλκέντεροσ; explicavit, in quadam epistula, quam ad eundem de Athenis scripserat, refert numquam se cibos Origene praesente sine lectione sumpsisse, nunquam venisse somnium, nisi e fratribus aliquis sacris litteris personaret, hoc diebus egisse vel noctibus, ut et lectio orationem susciperet et oratio lectionem.
passages.english: Ambrose, who supplied the paper, the expenses and the secretaries by which our truly 'Adamantius' and 'Chalkenteros' produced so countless a number of books, relates in a certain letter which he had written to him from Athens that he never took food in Origen's presence without reading, and never went to sleep unless one of the brothers was sounding forth the sacred writings; and that they did this day and night, so that reading followed upon prayer and prayer upon reading.
passages.notes: Adamantius ('man of adamant') was Origen's byname; Chalkenteros ('bronze-guts') was a Greek byname for tireless scholars such as Didymus. 'somnium' (dream) appears to stand for 'somnum' (sleep); translated as sleep. 'de Athenis' may be corrupt (the letter is usually placed elsewhere).

passages.original: Senectus vero—rursus admoneo—eorum, qui adulescentiam suam honestis artibus instruxerunt et in lege domini meditati sunt die ac nocte, aetate fit doctior, usu tritior, processu temporis sapientior et veterum studiorum dulcissimos fructos metit. Unde et sapiens ille Graeciae, cum expletis centum et septem annis se mori cerneret, dixisse fertur dolere, quod tunc egrederetur e vita, quando sapere coepisset; Plato octogesimo et uno anno scribens est mortuus; Isocrates nonaginta et novem annos in docendi scribendique labore conplevit; taceo ceteros philosophos, Pythagoram, Democritum, Xeno-cratem, Zenonem, Cleanthem, qui iam aetate longaeva in sapientiae studiis floruerunt: ad poetas venio,Homerum,Hesiodum, Simonidem,Stesichorum, qui grandes natu cygneum nescio quid et solito dulcius vicina morte cecinerunt.
passages.english: But the old age—I remind you again—of those who have equipped their youth with honourable arts and have meditated on the law of the Lord day and night becomes more learned with age, more practised with use, wiser with the passage of time, and reaps the sweetest fruits of its former studies. Hence that wise man of Greece too, when he saw that he was dying after completing a hundred and seven years, is said to have declared that he grieved that he was leaving life just when he had begun to be wise. Plato died writing in his eighty-first year; Isocrates completed ninety-nine years in the labour of teaching and writing; I pass over the other philosophers, Pythagoras, Democritus, Xenocrates, Zeno, Cleanthes, who flourished in the pursuit of wisdom when already of great age. I come to the poets, Homer, Hesiod, Simonides, Stesichorus, who, when advanced in years, sang some swan-song or other, sweeter than usual, as death drew near.
passages.notes: The 'wise man of Greece' is unnamed here (traditionally Theophrastus). 'fructos' read as 'fructus'.

passages.original: Sophocles, cum propter nimiam senectutem et rei familiaris neglegentiam a filiis accusaretur amentiae, Oedipi fabulam, quam nuper scripserat, recitavit iudicibus et tantum sapientiae in aetate iam fracta specimen dedit, ut severitatem tribunalium in theatri favorem verteret. Nec mirum, cum etiam Cato, Romani generis disertissimus, censorius iam et senex, Graecas litteras nec erubuerit nec desperaverit discere. Certe Homerus refert, quod de lingua Nestoris iam vetuli et paene decrepiti dulcior melle oratio fluxerit. Sed et ipsius Abisag nominis sacramentum sapientiam senum indicat ampliorem. Interpretatur enim pater meus superfluus vel patris mei rugitus.
passages.english: Sophocles, when on account of his extreme old age and his neglect of his household affairs he was accused of insanity by his sons, recited to the judges the play of Oedipus which he had recently written, and gave such proof of wisdom at an age already broken that he turned the severity of the court into the applause of a theatre. Nor is it surprising, since even Cato, the most eloquent of the Roman race, already an ex-censor and an old man, was neither ashamed nor despaired of learning Greek letters. Certainly Homer relates that from the tongue of Nestor, already old and almost decrepit, flowed speech sweeter than honey. And the mystery of the very name Abishag points to the greater wisdom of the old. For it is interpreted 'my father, superabundant' or 'the roaring of my father'.

passages.original: Amplexetur me modo sapientia et Abisag nostra, quae numquam senescit, in meo requiescat sinu. Inpolluta est virginitatisque perpetuae et in similitudinem Mariae, cum cotidie generet semperque parturiat, incorrupta est. Hinc reor dixisse et apostolum spiritu ferventes et in evangelio dominum praedicasse, quod in fine mundi, quando iuxta prophetam Zachariam stultus pastor esse coeperit, sapientia decrescente refrigescet caritas multorum. Audi igitur, ut beatus Cyprianus ait, non diserta, sed fortia. Audi fratrem collegio, patrem senio, qui te ab incunabulis fidei usque ad perfectam ducat aetatem et per singulos gradus vivendi praecepta constituens in te ceteros erudiat.
passages.english: Let wisdom now embrace me, and let our Abishag, who never grows old, rest in my bosom. She is undefiled and of perpetual virginity, and, after the likeness of Mary, though she daily conceives and is always giving birth, she is uncorrupted. Hence, I think, the apostle too said 'fervent in spirit', and the Lord proclaimed in the gospel that at the end of the world, when, according to the prophet Zechariah, the foolish shepherd has begun to be, as wisdom decreases the love of many will grow cold. Hear, then, as the blessed Cyprian says, words not eloquent but strong. Hear a brother in fellowship, a father in age, who may lead you from the cradle of faith up to mature age, and, setting down rules of living for each stage, may instruct others in you.

passages.original: Sermo eius et omne convivium de scripturis aliquid proponere, libenter audire, respondere verecunde, recta suscipere, prava non acriter confutare, dispu- tantem contra se magis docere quam vincere et ingenuo pudore, qui ornabat aetatem, quid cuius esset, simpliciter confiteri; atque in hunc modum eruditionis gloriam declinando eruditissimus habebatur. Illud, aiebat, Tertulliani, istud Cypriani, hoc Lactantii, illud Hilarii est. Sic Minucius Felix, ita Victorinus, in hunc modum est locutus Arnobius. Me quoque, quia pro sodalitate avunculi diligebat, interdum proferebat in medium. Lectione quoque adsidua et meditatione diuturna pectus suum bibliothecam fecerat Christi.
passages.english: His conversation and every dinner-party [of his consisted in] putting forward something from the scriptures, listening willingly, answering modestly, accepting what was right, refuting what was wrong without harshness, teaching rather than defeating one who argued against him, and, with the frank modesty that adorned his age, simply acknowledging what belonged to whom; and in this way, by declining the glory of learning, he was held most learned. 'This', he would say, 'is Tertullian's, that Cyprian's, this Lactantius', that Hilary's. So Minucius Felix [says], thus Victorinus, in this way Arnobius has spoken.' Me too, because he loved me on account of my friendship with his uncle, he would sometimes bring forward. By constant reading and long meditation he had made his breast a library of Christ.

passages.original: Etenim inter eum, qui decem vixit annos, et illum, qui mille, postquam idem vitae finis advenerit et inrecusabilis mortis necessitas, transactum omne tantundem est, nisi quod magis senex onustus peccatorum fasce proficiscitur. Optima quaeque dies miseris mortalibus aevi Prima fugit, subeunt morbi tristisque senectus Et labor et durae rapit inclementia mortis. Naevius poeta Pati, inquit, necesse est multa mortalem mala. Unde et Niobam, qui multum fleverit in lapidem et in diversas bestias conversas alias et Hecubam in canem> commutatam finxit antiquitas, et Hesiodus natales hominum plangens gaudet in funere, prudenterque Ennius: Plebes, ait, in hoc regio 1 antistat loco: licet Lacrimare plebi, regi honeste non licet. Ut regi, sic episcopo, immo minus regi quam episcopo. Ille enim nolentibus praeest, hic volentibus; ille terrore subicit, hic servitute dominatur;
passages.english: For between the one who has lived ten years and the one who has lived a thousand, once the same end of life has come and the inescapable necessity of death, all that has passed is just the same, except that the old man sets out more heavily loaded with a burden of sins. "Each best day of life is the first to flee for wretched mortals; diseases come on, and gloomy old age, and toil, and the harshness of unyielding death snatches [them] away." The poet Naevius says: "A mortal must suffer many ills." Hence antiquity also imagined Niobe, because she wept much, turned into stone, and other women changed into various beasts, and Hecuba changed into a dog; and Hesiod, lamenting the births of men, rejoices at a funeral. And Ennius says wisely: "The common people have the advantage over a king in this respect: the commoner may weep, the king may not do so with propriety." As with a king, so with a bishop, indeed less so with a king than with a bishop. For the one rules the unwilling, the other the willing; the one subdues by terror, the other rules by service;
passages.notes: The verse quotation is Virgil, Georgics 3.66–68. The Latin has "qui multum fleverit" (masculine), presumably for "quae" referring to Niobe; "conversas alias" is translated as "other women changed". A stray ">" after "canem" and the footnote numeral "1" after "regio" are omitted. "In hoc regio... loco" is taken as "in this respect [compared] to a king"; the Ennius fragment is uncertain in wording.

passages.original: Quaerentibus nobis dignum tantae feminae habitaculum, cum ita solitudinem cuperet, ut diversorio Mariae carere nollet, ecce subito discurrentibus nuntiis oriens totus intremuit, ab ultima Maeotide inter glacialem Tanain et Massagetarum immanes populos, ubi Caucasi rupibus feras gentes Alexandri claustra cohibent, erupisse Hunorum examina, quae pernicibus equis huc illucque volitantia caedis pariter ac terroris cuncta conplerent. Aberat tunc Romanus exercitus et bellis civilibus in Italia tenebatur. Hanc gentem Herodotus refert sub Dario, rege Medorum, viginti annis Orientem tenuisse captivum et ab Aegyptiis atque Aethiopibus annuum exegisse vectigal. Avertat Iesus ab orbe Romano tales ultra bestias! Insperati ubique aderant et famam celeritate vincentes non religioni, non dignitatibus, non aetati, non vagienti miserebantur infantiae.
passages.english: While we were seeking a dwelling worthy of so great a woman—for she so desired solitude that she was unwilling to be without Mary's lodging-place—behold, suddenly, as messengers ran to and fro, the whole East trembled: from the farthest Maeotis, between the icy Tanais and the monstrous peoples of the Massagetae, where the barriers of Alexander restrain wild nations by the crags of the Caucasus, swarms of Huns had burst forth, which, flying hither and thither on swift horses, filled everything alike with slaughter and terror. The Roman army was away at that time, held in Italy by civil wars. Herodotus relates that under Darius, king of the Medes, this people held the East captive for twenty years and exacted a yearly tribute from the Egyptians and Ethiopians. May Jesus turn such beasts away from the Roman world henceforth! They were present everywhere unexpected, and outstripping report by their speed they had no pity on religion, on rank, on age, or on wailing infancy.
passages.notes: Maeotis is the Sea of Azov, Tanais the Don.

passages.original: Dum essem iuvenis et solitudinis me deserta vallarent, incentiva vitiorum ardoremque naturae ferre non poteram; quae cum crebris ieiuniis frangerem, mens tamen cogitationibus aestuabat. Ad quam edomandam cuidam fratri, qui ex Hebraeis crediderat, me in disciplinam dedi, ut post Quintiliani acumina Ciceronisque fluvios gravitatemque Frontonis et lenitatem Plinii alphabetum discerem, stridentia anhelantiaque verba meditarer. Quid ibi laboris insumpserim, quid sustinuerim difficultatis, quotiens desperaverim quotiensque cessaverim et contentione discendi rursus inceperim, testis est conscientia tam mea, qui passus sum, quam eorum, qui mecum duxere vitam.
passages.english: While I was young and the wastes of the desert hemmed me in, I could not bear the incitements of vice and the heat of nature; though I broke them with frequent fasts, my mind still seethed with thoughts. To tame it, I put myself under the instruction of a certain brother who had come to believe from among the Hebrews, so that after the subtleties of Quintilian, the rivers of Cicero, the gravity of Fronto and the smoothness of Pliny, I might learn the alphabet and practise hissing and breathy words. What labour I spent on it, what difficulty I endured, how often I despaired, how often I gave up and, in my eagerness to learn, began again, my conscience is witness—both mine, who suffered it, and that of those who led their life with me.
